_comment: A hand-written extract for DESIGN.md 7.7.2: the class WEIGHTING, as opposed
to 7.7's class exclusion that modes.json covers.
Two ways between the same pair of points, and the shape is the whole test:
1  a RESIDENTIAL zigzag, SHORT   -- what shortest-distance picks
2  a PRIMARY sweep, LONGER       -- what a weighted cost picks
modes.json cannot serve for this, and the reason is worth stating: there the
big road is the SHORTER one (442 m of motorway against 1091 m of
residential), so shortest-distance already picks it and a weighting test
over that fixture could not fail. Here the big road must LOSE on distance
and WIN on cost, which is the only shape that can tell the two routers
apart.
The margin is deliberate, and it is measured rather than guessed. Residential
is weighted 1.50 and primary 0.85, so the break-even ratio is 1.76: past
that the zigzag wins again however big the road. The two candidate stretches
here are 984 m of zigzag against 1282 m of primary, a ratio of 1.30 -- so the
primary wins on cost by about 26%, and it loses on distance by 30%, which is
what makes this a test of the weighting and not of the router in general.
The first cut of this fixture was 1.65x, six per cent inside break-even. That
passes and it is a bad test: any tuning of the weight table would flip it,
and a test that fails when a constant moves by a hair is measuring the
constant rather than the behaviour.
Plus 3: a residential stub off the far end, so the destination is not itself
a junction of the two candidate ways -- a target that sat exactly where they
meet would let the snap pick either one and the assertion would flap.
Coordinates on a 0.001 degree grid near Asok, like the other fixtures.
